comments.text:

Assume they need care, claw back the money after if the investigation finds it was fraudulent or not necessary.

comments.text: About a month ago I had to go to the emergency room because I was dizzy and felt half out of it.  I was also shaking really bad, throwing up, and had numbness in my arm.  I never saw an actual doctor and the nurses did so many unnecessary things that didn't even make sense for my symptoms.  Throughout everything they did, they never once asked me how I felt or if I was getting less dizzy.  It was like I was just a body they could make money from.  I feel dizzy pretty much 24/7 and have passed out multiple times before, but I can't afford to see a specialist.  Now I'm stuck with a $2,500 medical bill and even though I have insurance, they will not cover any of it.  I'm currently trying to battle it out because I cannot afford the bill.  Thank you Dr. Mike for bringing awareness to this worldwide problem.  You are evident in your care for the patient over the profit.  I wish all doctors were like you! ❤

It felt like they knew that if they could hold out on the denials long enough, he'd be dead, and it would all be moot... and they were right. They stole hundreds and hundreds of hours the last hours I could have spent with him... and it made their shareholders a fraction of a penny for their trouble. Now their youngest child had a glioma of the optic nerve. Thankfully insurance is covering but still the out of pocket expenses are crazy. 
I used to work in health care as a PT. I got laid off when the BBA of 96 kicked in in 99 and crippled medicare. Those were reversed after people started dying from lack of care.

Medicare for all isn't perfect but better than what we have. We can spend billions on an illegal war but not provide even basic health care.

comments.text:
Just to highlight something, a doctor studies medicine for literal years, goes into residency to practice with professionals for years, and finally starts working on their own to provide healthcare to citizens, after over an entire decade of learning how to properly. They work closely with patients to determine exactly what type of care they NEED to function properly, and help send claims to insurance companies.

And a robot who has never met you, has no understanding of your illness, no feelings, and is literally programmed to make as much money as possible says: “No, you don’t need this medicine/treatment that a doctor who’s studied medicine and treatments for years is certain you need.”

People’s lives are not numbers on an income statement.

transcript: Meet Stephanie. She's a mother of four from North Carolina. She's a runner, an avid tennis player, and also went to war against her health insurance provider. Let's talk about that wild story and the tangible steps you can take when insurance company inevitably tries to screw you. If you live in America, it's not a matter if you'll need health insurance, but when. Unless your last name is Musk or Gates, you most likely won't be paying for your health care out of pocket. No, you'll be relying on America's hybrid health care system. You see, many countries around the world offer what's known as a single-payer system, where the government provides health care to its citizens free of charge, usually funded by taxes. The US is a bit different, running a hybrid system in which government-funded health care covers some people and others [music] are paid for by employers, individuals, or a combination of the three. It's rarely simple. And who manages all those claims? Mostly for-profit health insurance companies. Don't get me wrong. Just because something is for-profit does not automatically mean it's bad. And also, I'm not saying health care outside the US is perfect. Just ask someone from the UK or Canada how they feel about health care, and I'm sure they'll talk your ear off. But the US health insurance system is deeply and uniquely flawed. >> This morning, a young Kentucky man says his life is on hold because a heart condition left him with massive debt despite having health insurance. >> Medical bills from her breast cancer and his open-heart surgery nearly cost Mary McCurnin and her husband Ron their home. >> America spends more on health care than any other nation. >> Let's get back to Stephanie. In 2021, she noticed a weird spot on her arm. She went to the doctor and they agreed to run some tests. It probably wasn't a big deal. Meaningless spots pop up every day, right? Not this time. Stephanie was at Disney World with her family when she got a call from the doctor. That spot? Melanoma, the most serious form of skin cancer. And even worse, this was stage four with further testing revealing it the cancer had spread from that small spot on her elbow to her brain and lungs. She felt doomed. Fortunately, her husband's job provided Stephanie and their family with health insurance. It kicked in right away, paying for the care she needed to fight the disease. It wasn't easy, but after two years of treatment, Stephanie was recovering and the cancer was going away, but with a side [music] effect. The immunotherapy she was on started to have an impact on her joints. It became too painful to go up and down the stairs of her own house. She couldn't open a jar without crippling pain paralyzing her fingers or even grip a steering wheel to drive her own children to school. So, Stephanie had a tough decision to make. Stay on her immunotherapy to continue fighting her cancer or come off the therapy so her joints could return to normal. An impossible choice. Scared and confused, she went to two doctors and they both came to the same conclusion. Stephanie should stay on her therapy to keep fighting her cancer and relieve her joint pain with a drug called infliximab. God bless modern medicine. Unfortunately, Stephanie's insurance provider denied the medication saying infliximab didn't meet guidelines for coverage and was experimental. Surely this was a mistake. I mean, two different doctors said she needed the medication. So, Stephanie appealed and was denied. She appealed again and was denied then, too. She was back where she started. Cancer [music] or joint pain. Which would you choose? For most Americans, receiving a rejection and two denied appeals would be the end of the road. The insurance company had made it abundantly clear that Stephanie was on her own. But, it turns out she actually wasn't and neither are you. Zoom out with me for a second. There are over 300 million people living in the US and at one point or another, they're all going to need health coverage. This means a lot of appointments, a lot of claims, and a lot of cash exchanging hands. It's simply too much for any human system to process all on its own. So, most health insurance companies have started using AI and other computer systems to manage that chaos. And while that might sound efficient on paper, there are problems under the hood these companies don't want you to know about. Let me show you. First, do you know how a bank works? To put it simply, the bank promises to keep your money safe, so you deposit your cash and withdraw it when necessary. What some don't realize is that despite what your bank balance might say, your money might not physically be there. That's because the bank takes all the money from its customers and then uses it to pay salaries, give loans, invest, all sorts of things. Folks get alarmed by this, but it's actually how banks make money, and it's usually not a problem, especially because banks are FDIC insured. If you ever need your money, the bank will remember what you deposited and allow you to withdraw it, often drawing on funds from somebody else. At the end of the day, you still get your cash, so who cares if it isn't the same exact bills you deposited. But, what would happen if every single person who used that bank all showed up at the same time demanding their money? The bank wouldn't be able to give everyone every dollar they're owed because they've already spent a lot of it. This is called a run on banks, and it's one of the worst things that can happen during an economic collapse like the Great Depression of 1929, or when governments fall apart. A health insurance company operates in a similar way. For example, [music] let's create an an imaginary health insurance company called Mike Care, and I get 100 customers. Every month I charge each customer a monthly premium. Some of that money goes in my pocket for running the business, and the rest gets saved up for one of my customers gets sick or injured. Mike Care would pay for the treatment for that customer, and they'd ultimately get healthy. Well, that's a hyper-simplified version of a health insurance company, and of course, the reality gets a bit more complicated. What would I do at Mike Care if all 100 of my customers needed care at the same time? Well, the money I collected from premiums wouldn't be enough to pay for everyone, so I'd have to start setting some rules. Maybe one of the patients wants an elective procedure like plastic surgery, so I decide we aren't going to cover that. Perhaps My Care will agree to cover all expenses of health care only after the patient has paid 5,000 of their own. I'll call that the deductible. What if one of my customers is lying about the care that they need in a scam to get money? Insurance fraud. I've got to be on the lookout for that, too. Bottom line, I need to set some guardrails so that we have enough money in the coffers to provide care when people actually need it. Now and then, you'd see My Care start denying coverage. And in this very, very small-scale and simplified example, you can easily see why that's important. But, let's look at this at a bigger scale. Zoom out to what we actually see in the United States. What if My Care had millions of customers and millions of stockholders who owned pieces of my now publicly traded health insurance company? Well, on one hand, I'd be very rich from owning that stock. And as CEO, my responsibility would not actually be to provide solely good health care. It would be to provide a strong financial return to my shareholders and my end-of-year bonus. There would be incredible pressure to raise premium costs, deny coverage, or at the very least make it harder to get approvals. You know, shady stuff. So, as CEO of My Care, I have an idea. What if [music] I build an AI supercomputer to oversee the whole thing and tell it to just increase the rate of denials by just a few percentage points. You know, random rejections left and right, even if the patient is genuinely sick and our policy is supposed to cover them. Well, patients would file appeals, hire lawyers, and sue me for failing to hold up my end of the bargain, right? Actually, yes. That is right, but it only works if patients actually do it. This is the bet insurance companies are making. They're gambling that you will be overwhelmed, confused, defeated, and not [music] bother filing an appeal. In fact, they're just following basic statistics and human psychology. The more hoops they make you jump through, the less money they'll have to spend. [music] Health insurers routinely deny 850 million claims a year in the US, and less than 1% of people appeal a denial. That's a lot of profit that is likely not legitimate. But get this, when patients do appeal, they win over 50% of the time. This is why you'll hear me say, "Always argue the bill." Okay, Dr. Mike, so I'm ready to appeal my denial. How do I do that? Let me give you a list of everything you need to get your money. Stick with me through the end here, and I'll also give you a shortcut that can make this much easier. First, find the specific reason you were denied, whether that's not medically necessary, experimental, or step therapy required. Then, build your evidence file. This is all the documentation of what you've been through so far. Doctors' notes, prior authorizations, clinical research, and proof of everything you've already tried. Next, a lot of people assume that their approvals and denials are up to the whim of the insurance company. Wrong. For all the power health insurers have in the United States, they [music] aren't God. There are laws in place meant to protect you from predatory behavior. Quite often, when they deny your claim, they're breaking the law, and that's something you need to remind them of.
